item.title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics (136 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics/, See on Hacker News

Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI.

You can see this leap in capability on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark, which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model.

As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas:

  • Robot control → Mobile manipulation with MuJoCo practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models.
  • Real2Sim → Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches.
  • Physical understanding → Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation.
  • Research and self-improvement → Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware.

Unlocking robot control with Argon

1. Spot mobile manipulation: Putting in the trash bin with MuJoCo practice

Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin.

Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside.

Prompt:

There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left.
Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin.
Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing.

Plain text

Copied

2. Zero-shot control

Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns.

Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle.

Prompt:

[Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json]

Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug.

## Execution Discipline
- Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`.

## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png)
- `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base
- `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left         | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right
- `+Z`: Height above table                | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`)
- `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center
- `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line
- `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y)
- `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis

## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow
1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`:
   `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`).
2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1:
   - Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done`
   - Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done`
   - Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done`
3. Send motion primitives (`POST /plan`) and verify visually after every turn in the updated `wrist_cam.png`. If `status == "grasp_failed"`, call `robot.look_at(...)` to re-observe and recover closed-loop.

## Code-as-Policies Primitives (`POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/plan`)
robot.look_at(x=0.35, y=0.13, z=0.14, grid_z=0.015)
x, y = robot.deproject(u=0.52, v=0.48, z_plane=0.015)
robot.grasp(x=x, y=y, z=0.015, yaw_deg=-35, pitch_deg=90)
robot.place(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.075)
robot.place_until_contact(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.015, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002)
robot.goto(x=0.28, y=0.05, z=0.04, arc_z=0.14, pitch_deg=25, azimuth_deg=90, roll_deg=0, speed=0.10)
robot.move_by(forward=0.025, dz=-0.002, dpitch_deg=-3, droll_deg=5, speed=0.04)
robot.move_until_contact(dz=-0.06, speed=0.03, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002)
robot.open_gripper() / robot.close_gripper() / robot.home() / robot.done()

3. Omni control

Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles (G, R, A, N, O) into a clean row spelling A - R - G - O - N. Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts.

Iterative Video World Model Steering Dexterous Hands: 33-Step Steered Video Rollout Spelling A-R-G-O-N.

Prompt:

Goal: {task_goal}

You are steering a video world model (Gemini Omni) in an iterative visual feedback loop. Inspect the attached frames from the latest rollout and write the next timestamped action prompt for the video world model:
- Break complex motions into one simple, single-direction action at a time.
- Keep inactive hands retracted and avoid blocking the camera's view of objects in the workspace.
- Explicitly state which areas of the workspace become empty after an object moves.
- Use [MM:SS.mmm] timestamps for each action beat and wrap your output in <omni_prompt> tags.

Example format (sample timestamps only, not the full prompt):
<omni_prompt>
[00:00.000] Character A's left hand rests at the side while the right hand reaches toward the target object.
[00:02.500] Character A's right fingertips push the object smoothly into the center of the table, leaving its starting area empty.
[00:05.000] Character A's right hand opens and retracts to the side so all placed objects remain in clear view of the camera.
</omni_prompt>

Plain text

Copied

Unlocking Real2Sim with Argon

1. Robot view to simulation

Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop.

Left (Real View): synchronized real robot camera feeds; Right (Simulated): 3D MuJoCo scene reconstructed and calibrated by Argon.

Prompt:

[Attached: robot_rollout_episode]

Build a MuJoCo scene of the robot and reconstructed task objects. When each episode is replayed frame by frame, by driving the robot joints toward the logged observation.state with joint-space PD.

Iterate using two verification objectives:
(1) Visual match: MuJoCo renders from the head_left, left_wrist, and right_wrist cameras line up with, and look like, those real observations.
(2) Physical match: the simulated contact force/torque on each Sharpa fingertip, in the sensor frame, matches the logged tactile_force in timing, magnitude and direction.

What you can tune happens before simulation starts:
(1) Static object assets: realistic geometry, collision shapes, mass, inertia, friction and joints, with appearance close to the real objects, plus the initial object poses at t = 0.
(2) Offline-planned robot commands, changed only in frames where the real fingertips are near an object. Each command must stay within 0.55 rad (arm joints) and 0.65 rad (hand joints) of the logged teleop trajectory. Everywhere else, replay the logged trajectory unchanged.

No sim cheating: task objects may move only through real MuJoCo contact with the robot hands and the environment (mj_step).
Not allowed after t = 0: changing MjModel parameters; applying external forces or torques to objects; welds or equality constraints; feedforward torques beyond joint-space PD; setting or rolling back object qpos/qvel; disabling or excluding collisions; reporting contact forces that don't come from the MuJoCo solver (for example, copying the logged tactile readings).

Immediately present the reconstructed scene and rollout results as an interactive HTML session viewer with one page per episode, showing:
- At the bottom: A synced timeline (play, scrub, speed control) that drives every panel.
- On the left panel: An interactive 3D Blender scene showing the simulated robot and objects, showing contact points and force arrows as replay progresses.
- On the right panel: Real vs. sim camera views side by side for all 3 cameras. Real vs. sim finger force visualizations.

Plain text

Copied

2. Human view to simulation

Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics.

Human View to Simulation — Egocentric Human Video to Dexterous Humanoid Twin: Left shows the input egocentric human RGB video; Right shows the synchronized 500 Hz MuJoCo + Blender Cycles multi-view simulation rollout.

Prompt:

[Attached: egocentric_human_video.mp4, candidate_sim_views.png, hand_3d_keypoints.json]

You are building a physically solvable 500 Hz MuJoCo manipulation environment (`scene.xml`) and studio Blender render that faithfully reproduces the tabletop task shown in `egocentric_human_video.mp4` on a bimanual humanoid robot with 22-DoF dexterous five-fingered hands:

1. Scene Reconstruction & Camera Calibration:
   - Identify only the manipulation-relevant objects (the grasped target object and the receiving container or landmark) and triangulate their 3D tabletop coordinates from the egocentric camera intrinsics/extrinsics.
   - Replace crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed 3D meshes so concave containers (nested bowls, recessed wooden trays, open bins) support physical interior placement.

2. 500 Hz Dexterous Motion-Fitting Stress Test:
   - Retarget the 3D human wrist and finger keypoints to the humanoid's 7-DoF arm and 22-DoF hand joints, and step the trajectory in MuJoCo at 500 Hz (dt = 0.002s) with zero kinematic weld constraints.
   - Verify opposing thumb-and-finger force closure, clean object lift (> 2 cm), and stable final placement inside or beside the target landmark.

Plain text

Copied

3. Sketch to simulation

With Argon, a developer can snap a photo of a rough pen-and-paper sketch—showing an Apollo 2 humanoid throwing a ball along a parabolic arc to topple a 3-2-1 stack of boxes on a table—and have Argon automatically construct the GPU-accelerated mujoco_warp scene, synthesize a balanced 76-DoF whole-body and five-finger throw trajectory, verify 6/6 target knockdown in closed-loop physics, and export a Blender 4.5 Cycles render.

Sketch to Simulation — Hand-Drawn Sketch to Dexterous Humanoid Trajectory & Cycles Render.

Prompt:

[Attached: hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg]

Translate this hand-drawn sketch into a physically verified humanoid simulation in `mujoco_warp` and a raytraced Blender Cycles video:

1. Scene & Kinematic Setup from Sketch:
   - Parse the spatial layout from `hand_drawn_throw_sketch.jpg`: place the 76-DoF humanoid (32-DoF body equipped with two 22-DoF five-finger dexterous hands) at the origin facing a table holding a 3-2-1 pyramid of 6 rigid target boxes, with a projectile sphere grasped in the right five-finger hand.

2. Whole-Body Balance & Dexterous Throw Synthesis:
   - Synthesize a 50 Hz whole-body throwing trajectory (140 steps, 2.80 s) across four phases: (1) stable stance & 5-finger power grasp closure, (2) torso/shoulder wind-up with ankle-hip Center-of-Mass compensation, (3) forward whipping acceleration, and (4) synchronized 22-DoF five-finger opening at peak hand velocity so the ball launches on a ballistic arc into the pyramid's second-tier center of mass.
   - Verify in `mujoco_warp` contact physics that the humanoid maintains upright balance (< 3 cm pelvis drift) and knocks down all 6 target boxes.

Plain text

Copied

Unlocking physical understanding with Argon

1. Hindsight labeling and data quality

Argon has precise physical understanding of dexterous manipulation and can provide detailed segmentation and text labeling from video. Argon is able to identify poor manipulation segments such as pauses, unstable grasps and fumbles. Given an overhead video of a bimanual ALOHA 2 robot folding a square sheet of paper into an origami fox over 136 seconds, Argon produces a time-aligned 4-level hindsight annotation hierarchy: Episode Goal (G1), 6 contiguous Semantic Subtasks (G2), 17 contact-level Atomic Primitives (G3), and automated Quality Control (QC) reweighting that holds task progress flat during fumbles and retries.

Argon Multi-Granularity Hindsight & Telemetry HUD.

Prompt:

[Attached: Aloha2_Origami_20250309.mp4]

Produce a time-aligned multi-granularity hindsight annotation JSON with four levels:
1. G1_episode_instruction: Concise imperative sentence describing the overall manipulation goal.
2. G2_subtasks: Contiguous semantic subtask phases specifying which arm(s) anchor vs. fold/rotate the object.
3. G3_atomic_primitives: Fine-grained contact-level primitives (3–15s) aligned with grasp closure, crease sweeps, release, or retry attempts.
4. quality_control_and_reweighting: Hold task_progress_pct flat during non-progressing slip/delamination retry loops and downweight them (0.15x–0.25x) for Behavior Cloning.

Plain text

Copied

2. Find the odd ball

To recreate the classic 12-ball balance scale puzzle with robots, Argon builds a bimanual Franka FR3 MuJoCo environment with 12 visually identical pool balls (one secretly heavier or lighter) and an articulated Roberval two-pan balance scale. It then writes a vision-only closed-loop solver that triangulates the balls from stereo RGB cameras, visually reads the scale tilt after each weighing, and isolates the odd ball into the Heavy (Red) or Light (Blue) tray within 3 weighings.

Find the Odd Ball (Vision-Only Closed-Loop Solver): Dual-arm Franka FR3 weighing candidate balls on the Gold/Teal pans, reading stereo scale tilt , and isolating the confirmed Heavy odd ball into the Red tray in 3 weighings.

Prompt:

# Prompt 1 — Physics-Accurate MuJoCo Environment & Benchmark Generation
Make a MuJoCo environment where a dual-arm robot (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers on a shared tabletop) is tasked to solve the classic 12-ball balance scale weight puzzle from https://www.mathsisfun.com/pool_balls_solution.html.
1. Create 12 visually indistinguishable pool balls in a 2x6 starting rack (11 standard 150 g, 1 odd ball either 270 g or 30 g).
2. Build a functional two-pan Roberval balance scale at the center of the table with parallelogram equality constraints (`mjEQ_JOINT`) so the Left (Gold) and Right (Teal) pans stay horizontal, plus Red (Heavy) and Blue (Light) submission trays.
3. Track distinct settled weighings (`weighing_count`) and reward `1.00` for isolating the true odd ball in the correct Heavy/Light tray within <= 3 weighings.

# Prompt 2 — Closed-Loop Vision-Only Solver
Implement an independent closed-loop policy relying strictly on stereo RGB camera inputs (`head_camera_left_rgb_image`, `head_camera_right_rgb_image`) and robot proprioception (`add_privileged_task_observations=False`):
1. Segment the 12 balls, Gold/Teal pans, and Red/Blue trays in both stereo views and triangulate their 3D coordinates.
2. Visually read the balance scale tilt after each weighing from stereo vertical pixel disparity (+1 = left heavier, -1 = right heavier, 0 = balanced).
3. Rotate the gripper wrist yaw by 90 degrees when grasping/placing inside the narrow scale pans to clear the raised rims, and isolate the odd ball into the Red or Blue tray within <= 3 weighings.

Plain text

Copied

3. Value function

Argon is a general value function for robotics tasks. Evaluated on a 60-second bimanual ring-sorting episode from a human UMI dataset, Argon iteratively inspects synchronized head, left-gripper, and right-gripper camera feeds around contact transitions to generate dense value function / task progress predictions and decompose the trajectory into 28 segments with positive, neutral, and negative progress slopes.

Value Function: Synchronized 3-camera UMI playback (head, left gripper, right gripper) locked to animated task progress curve and bimanual segment annotations.

Prompt:

[Attached: umi_head.mp4, umi_left_gripper.mp4, umi_right_gripper.mp4]

Look at 3 videos of human wearing a gripper performing activities from head, left, right gripper views. Look at the videos thoroughly and give a detailed plot of progress at the task (with positive, neutral, negative slope), identifying important segments in the video and labeling the activities. Look at individual frames or subsegments of the video if necessary to get a better understanding.

Plain text

Copied

Unlocking research and self-improvement with Argon

1. Action improvement via simulation

Argon can generate new data in simulation to improve performance of generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models. Starting from a single RGB photo of the real tabletop, Argon autonomously builds a calibrated MuJoCo simulation twin, defines new tasks, and synthesizes a closed-loop motion generator to collect 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes in simulation—boosting real-world physical robot Success Rate from 56% to 75% and reducing completion time from 35s to 24s.

Action Improvement via Simulation: improves the real-world evaluation benchmark (56% → 75% Success Rate and 35s → 24s Completion Time).

Prompt:

[Attached: real_tabletop_photo.jpg]

You are given a single overhead RGB camera photo (`real_tabletop_photo.jpg`) of a bimanual robot workspace (two 7-DoF Franka FR3 arms with parallel-jaw grippers and 4 RGB cameras) facing a table arranged with photobooth party props.
1. Reconstruct procedural 3D meshes and compound MuJoCo collision primitives for all 9 party props matching their real-world dimensions, colors, and resting poses, including spring-hinged deformable crown panels for the soft plush cap.
2. Define a 77-task single-arm and bimanual curriculum (pick-and-place, uprighting, directional pushing, mid-air handovers, bimanual scoop-and-push, and pipelined table clearing).
3. Synthesize a closed-loop IK trajectory generator across ±10 cm pose randomization, verify `reward == 1.0` in MuJoCo physics, and export 4,500+ episodes for VLA fine-tuning.

Plain text

Copied

2. Self-Improvement for visual pick and place

On a simple 6-DoF arm, Argon iteratively self-improves both execution speed and placement accuracy on a pick and place task via trial and self-reflection.

SO-101 Vision-Guided Pick-and-Place — Iterative Hardware Self-Improvement Across Iterations 1 → 2 → 3: Iteration 1 (58.9s), Iteration 2 (22.9s, grazed box rim on drop), and Iteration 3 (17.4s, dead-center drop).

Prompt:

# Stage 1 — Measure Objects & Dry-Run Plan (No Hardware Motion)
Stage 1: measure objects — find the objects and plan the whole motion. The arm does not move in this stage.

A. I put a LEGO brick and a box on the table in front of the arm, and the wooden box to one side. Find the brick and the wooden box in the image. And also in the real world. Show this in an annotated image.

B. A dry-run plan (no hardware). Write the planner to pick and place the lego block. Print the plan table, draw all poses onto the overhead image, and stop. Do not move the robot.
Report with evidence.

# Stage 2 — Pre-Pick Hover & Wrist-Camera Verification
Stage 2: Put the gripper above the brick without touching it, and verify with the wrist camera that the arm and the vision agree. Please record executions with both cameras (compressed video is OK).

# Stage 3 (Autonomous Pick-and-Place → Self-Improvement → Optimization):
1. Execute autonomously: Turn the Stage 1 dry run into a real grasp, lift, and place into the wooden box. Run it yourself subject to safety rules from AGENTS.md.

2. Self-improve: When an attempt fails, diagnose it yourself. Review your own logs and wrist/overhead footage, find the root cause, check the fix in a dry run, and retry.

3. Optimize on feedback: Once it succeeds, make it at least 2× faster within safety limits (rule R5) unless I authorize more, or give feedback.

Plain text

Copied

3. One-prompt robotics paper reproductions in MuJoCo WebAssembly

With a single prompt per paper, Argon reads a robotics control manuscript and any released checkpoints, ports the physics model and closed-loop controller (from 7-network hierarchical locomotion in DeepLoco and 50 Hz PPO actors in HUSKY to Web Worker iLQR in Whole-Body MPC) into self-contained MuJoCo WebAssembly browser labs, and verifies them in headless Chromium.

Five Landmark Legged & Humanoid Papers Running Live in Browser (MuJoCo WASM): Robotic Soccer OP3 1v1, DeepLoco, Massively Parallel Deep RL ANYmal C, Whole-Body MPC Go2, and HUSKY G1 Skateboarding (from 68 interactive browser sandboxes reproduced by Argon).

Prompt:

[Attached: paper.pdf, optional author_checkpoints/ or urdf_assets/]

Reproduce the paper "<Paper Title & arXiv ID>" from scratch in MuJoCo WebAssembly and deploy a self-contained browser lab + visual essay:
1. Match the paper's exact physics timestep, actuator gains (kp/kv), torque limits, and kinematic constraints in MuJoCo XML, and run real neural inference or Web Worker iLQR in JavaScript at the paper's exact control rates.
2. Build `index.html` (Spatial UI simulator with camera presets, live telemetry plots, and disturbance injection) and `scrollytelling.html` (interactive visual essay).
3. Run a headless Chromium (Playwright) verification loop asserting 0 console errors and non-zero task progress over 300+ frames.

Plain text

Copied

Advancing embodied intelligence with Argon

Argon bridges coding, visual perception, physics simulation, and embodied robot control. By reasoning natively over multi-view video, 3D geometry, contact mechanics, and proprioceptive telemetry, Argon understands not just what objects are in a scene, but how they physically interact with agents to accomplish whole-body dexterous tasks. Gemini 4 Argon marks an important milestone accelerating the path toward physical AGI. By building this core intelligence, our goal is to enable robotics that can work alongside humans to solve complex challenges.

Getting started

You can start building with Gemini 4 Argon today across Google’s developer platforms:

  • Google AI Studio: Available to Google AI Ultra subscribers.
  • Gemini API: Available with the paid tier of the Gemini API in AI Studio. Use gemini-4-argon in the Interactions API with day-one support across the google-genai SDKs.
  • Google Antigravity: Available for Google AI Ultra subscribers. To start building, select Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) as your active model in Google Antigravity for complex planning, /goal runs, and multi-agent orchestration.

item.title: Cyberattack halts construction of tunnel between Denmark and Germany (135 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ua.news/en/world/kiberataka-zupinila-budivnitstvo-tuneliu-mizh-daniieiu-ta-nimechchinoiu-rmf24, See on Hacker News

Construction of a road-and-rail tunnel under the Fehmarn Belt strait, intended to connect Denmark and Germany, has stopped due to a cyberattack. The incident affected the international FLC consortium carrying out work on the project, RMF24 reports.

Equipment and workers’ access blocked

As a result of the attack, workers’ identification cards stopped functioning. Vessels, cranes and platforms used for offshore work were also immobilized. According to Danish media, construction work has therefore been completely halted.

The FLC consortium employs around 2,800 people in total from companies in Denmark, Germany, France, Belgium and the Netherlands. There is a significant number of Poles among the workers at the site.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Details of the attack are being established

Representatives of the investor company Sund & Baelt confirmed that they are discussing the situation with the contractor. It has not yet been established who exactly is behind the cyberattack or how long it will take to eliminate its consequences.

Henning Mortensen, head of the Danish Council for Digital Security, did not rule out a connection between the incident and hybrid warfare. In recent weeks, Danish services have warned of possible cyberattacks from Russia and raised the threat level to high.

The 18-kilometer tunnel is being built from 89 concrete elements, which are transported and connected at sea using digital software. The project’s cost is estimated at approximately €7 billion. Its opening was initially planned for 2029, but possible delays had already been reported earlier.

item.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic (296 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control, See on Hacker News

At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.

Growing our monorepo

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.

As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.

Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?

Principles for agent-scale source control

With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling, so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:

Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.

Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.

A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.

Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.

Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.

The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.

How Scion works

It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.

Data structures

In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.

This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.

A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.

This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.

Scaling Scion

A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.

Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.

Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.

In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.

The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.

Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.

What we learned building Scion

We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.

Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.

What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.

Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future.

Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code.

We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day.

We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes.

A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.

We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them.

Contributing to the wider ecosystem

We see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case.

Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities.

Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful.

However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well.

Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential.

Acknowledgements

Written by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique.

Footnotes

  1. Storing changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo.

1. I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI BOT traffic

For the past few years, I've been working on sprinklz.io, a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed.

A month ago, I posted it to HN, and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then…

My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse several days after my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load.

So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!).

Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one specific user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked.

Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc.

The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that can day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users.

P.S. if you'd like to check it out, the website is fully free, and available here

The TLDR is that it lets you define your own customizations, in addition to things like the points totals from hacker news. You can use it to filter out topics, like AI or LLMs, but the topics are completely arbitrary and you can program your own customizations.

2. Using LLMs to Make the Emacs Web Browser Great Again

When I tell people about the emacs web browser, their first reaction is 'Wait emacs has a web browser?!', followed by, 'yeah… I guess that's kind of a web browser'.

The emacs web browser is designed to render webpages in a terminal-based, textonly environment and, well, it goes about exactly the way you'd expect. It works well on HTML-only, small-content websites, but not so good for anything else.

The problem is that emacs is primarily a text-only editor, but the modern internet is very much not plain-text based. Simple HTML, designed in the simple style of the 1990s has a clear translation into plain text, but modern UI design, with it's visual styling, heavy javascript, and just, overall chaos, not so much.

The emacs web browser would be great, if only we could find a way to go back in time…

Ok, so the plan is simple. We take modern webpages, rewrite their source code into old-school simply-styled HTML, and then pipe it through to the emacs web browser. We just need to find a way to do this easily and at scale.

So um, you didn't forget about LLMs did you? It's nice to be using them in a way that will hopefully reduce the amount of spam content in the world.

Basically, the plan is we write a program that:

  • Opens a webpage in firefox
  • Loads the page and runs all the javascript
  • Asks an LLM to generate a re-usable program that transforms the current-page's contents into simplified text
  • Inject the generated javascript into the firefox browser
  • Grab the new page source and forward it to emacs web browser.

Yeah, and so, I've been using it, and it runs very well. Like realistically I can use this on many webpages where eww (emacs web wowser) did not run previously.

Below are some examples of before and after:

The docs for Clojure's mapcat

Figure 1: (before) Using eww-readable

Figure 2: (after) Using simpleweb-simplify-page

It takes a moment to generate the initial modifier program, but once it's generated, it runs pretty fast, and during day-to-day browsing, it mostly doesn't need any extra LLM calls. I have been using it myself and enjoying the experience.

The source code lives here: https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb

and is open-source, and free to install, etc., etc.

2. If technology got better, why did everything get worse?

I think we all know the answer to this: bad incentives.

Technology makes systems more productive, but it does not, in fact, make you in particular more productive. The tools that enable computers to be more efficient also enable people to be more efficient at exploiting your time, attention, and wellbeing. I'm talking neural nets babyyy.

I first noticed the problem in 2018. Or rather, I noticed that I had a problem, and that problem was spendinng 3 hours a day watching starcraft 2 replays and wondering where the time went, and how I managed to stay up til 2am again.

What's interesting to me is that I didn't have any of these problems until the late 2010s. I had a computer with an internet connection since at least the mid 2000s, and a smartphone with twitter and reddit and the like not long after. It's possible that I've gotten less resiliant over the years, but I have a sneaking suspiscion that it's the computers who changed.

I can't quite put my finger on it, but I have this sensation that every time I interact with a system or website, I'm playing this kind of adversarial game, where I'm trying to just go about my day, and maybe read a little article about computers, and they're trying to figure out a way to keep me on their site for just a little bit longer.

I also have this feeling that as software engineering has moved from a discipline of hobbyists and enthusiasts to leaders who increasingly developed through finance or business-minded tracks, we've found ourselves with these major tools that we used to love become both extremely bland and extremely profitable.

So what can we do it make it stop?

  1. touch grass. really when the world is like this, i think the best solution is to just leave. it's not easy, especially when the planning is often online, but if you can set it up, I promise that a day in the park playing chess with your friends is better than any amount of time you can spend on the internet.
  2. take to the streets. i think that protesting is effective, and more people should do it. if you're willing to take action, it models to others that they can take action.
  3. stop coming back to the same machines. I think we all have this gamblers fallacy in us, where if it didn't pay out the first time, but it pays out sometimes, we try the machine again, but it doesn't really work like that. if you're losing money the lesson is to stop putting coins in the machine.

editor's note: I've been working on a free customizable news reader as a way to take out some of my frustrations with the modern internet. if you don't use this one, I recommend following individual blogs and websites, because it's so much better to just get off these big platforms entirely.

editors note 2: i haven't yet posted this latest article to my rss xml, because i'm not ready to send notifications for it yet. will add in the coming weeks.

3. Deft version 0.2.0

Now that deft 0.2.0 is released, I figure it's a good time to talk about what I built, and why I built it.

The point of Clojure's everything-is-a-map toolkit is that getters and setters are a waste of time. Clojure was built, in large part, in response to the crappy 2008 Java workflow, where you had to write getters, setters, and builders, and you took on all this bloat that nobody enjoyed.

The problem is that if you want to represent your data using the built-in defprotocol and defrecord, and you want to define functions that depend on the presence of a certain field, then the only way to encode that information into the protocol is to add getter and setter metohds to it. icky.

You can also use a combination of protocol + malli schema to represent this, but then when you use it, you need to specify 'this function takes as input something that both implements this protocol and implements this Malli schema'. Also icky.

What we want is something we can use in the style of defprotocol and defrecord, but gives us all the getters and setters and map-like stuff by default. The key insight is that if a field exists in a record, we get all the other good stuff, so we just need to add support for protocols with required keys.

Deft v0.2.0 adds support for namespaced keys in type and protocol definitions. i.e., you can now do: 

(defp Positioned :required-keys [::pos - ::Point])

and 

(deft Circle [::location/position radius])

(>Circle ::location/position [1 2] :radius 12)

this is useful because you can now define methods that depend on those fields being present i.e.: 

(defp Gremlin :extends [location/Positioned])

(defmethod game-object/get-hitbox ::Gremlin [self]
  (js/Matter.Bodies.rectangle
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/x])
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/y])
   15 15))

I finished reading On the Edge last week, and it was bad. Not that I don't respect Nate Silver. I respect him a lot. So when his seminal text on gambling and risk taking was a rambling mess, I was suprised and disappointed. Nevertheless, a completionist at heart, I trudged on, to the very end, where I was greeted with this message:

"ChatGPT was a significant help in writing this book, serving as a creative muse when coming up with things like chapter subheadings, metaphors, and analogies, and for refining my understanding of technical topics that are likely to be well represented in its corpus."

Technically he wrote the book by hand, and technically he typed the letters onto his keyboard, but you know, did he really? Did he put his whole thought and mind and being into every word on the page? Maybe. I'm reminded of the absolute classic [Simple Made Easy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SxdOUGdseq4), a video where so much of the core lecture is built on defining precise language, and saying exactly what you mean. When you offload that work, you don't just skip word choices, you skip that thinking, and you miss out on that organization and mental clarity.

In reading Nate's book, there's a real and noticeable difference between the language that feels baked into the organizational fabric of Nate's mentality, and the bits that were added on as an afterthought. The later chapters especially felt like they lacked that sort of mental compactification that cohesifies everything under one vision. I'm sad because this could have been a phenominal work, and it's clear that a lot of effort was made, especially into interviews and data collection, and it feels like it's just lacking that one last missing piece of insight to bring it all the way home.

So how much LLMs is too much LLMs? Well, when it comes to human connection, I'd say the answer is near zero. I don't want to read your AI generated e-mails, and I certainly don't want to read your AI generated essays. I'd much rather read your prompt instead, because I care about what you, yes, you personally think about, and I want to understand what you wanted to communicate.

Don't get me wrong, I love LLMs for the right purpose. I'd love to use LLMs on doctor's notes to build models that predict whether the flu is spreading. But when it comes to writing, especially this kind of writing, it just feels so unnecessary, because when you write down your thoughts, I already have exactly what I wanted, and it just feels so silly to add an extra stop in between.

As a poker player and game theorist, I'm sure Nate would appreciate the phrase "If you couldn't be bothered to write it, then I can't be bothered to read it". And you know, despite a belief that art can live separately from the artist, deep down for me this claim rings true. Not that the same words produced by a person are inherently different than the same words from an LLM, but it throws off my little Bayesian estimator a little.

If the smartest person I know spent 10,000 hours writing, editing, polishing, and publishing a 500 page novel, it tells me not just that the smartest person I know had some thoughts on a topic, but it tells me that they decided to spend 10,000 hours of their precious time, and of their precious energy to communicate this idea to me. It feels good that the time it took me to read it is porportional (and usually less than) the time it took you to write it, because it shows me that you care about the time and energy of creating this exchange.

And it's not just fully AI generated slop that hits this barrier. When you incorporate LLMs into your writing, even a little bit, you miss out on the ability to process your thoughts and create human connection.

5. Building Chess in about 350 lines of Clojure

I recently released deft, a Clojure library that defines types and protocols using plain maps, and so, to take it for a spin, I wrote the game of chess in Clojure.

Chess is a good trial run for any class and interface system, because it's reasonably small and self-contained (and has some pretty obvious choice for classes), but it also comes with some of the messiness of a real application, in that, you want to write something concise, but you still have to handle edge-cases, like castling and en passant.

I hand-drew all of the pieces, and used this little reagent snippet to render the display, 

[:h-box
 (doall (for [x (range (count tiles))]
                  ^{:key x}
                  [:v-box
                   (doall (for [y (reverse (range (count (nth tiles x))))]
                     ^{:key y}
                     [:p {:style {:background-color (cond
                                                      (= [x y] @currently-selected-location)  "yellow"
                                                      (= (mod (+ x y) 2) 1) "white"
                                                      :else "black")
                                  :height "4rem"
                                  :width "4rem"
                                  }
                           :on-click (fn [] (move-selected-piece
                                                    game-board-atom
                                                    currently-selected-location
                                                    [x y]))}

                      (if (not (nil? (get-in tiles [x y])))
                        [:img {:src (image-path (::piece-type (get-in tiles [x y])))
                               :style {:height "100%"
                                       :width "100%"
                                       :filter (when (= (::color (get-in tiles [x y])) ::black)
                                                 "invert()")}}]
                        "")]))]))]

but kind of the interesting bit is how to represent the board state and all of its pieces.

I did sort of the obvious thing, and defined types representing a chess piece, and then a board, as a 8x8 grid of pieces 

(deft ChessPiece [color piece-type])


(deft ChessBoard [tiles - [:vector [:vector [:or :nil ChessPiece]]]
                  curr-move - [:enum ::white ::black]
                  move-history - [:vector ChessMove]])

and then for the piece behavior, I made protocols that define how a piece is displayed, and how it can move. 

(defp PieceType
  (image-path [this]))

(defp MovablePiece
  (is-valid-move-for-piece? [this game-board start-location end-location]))

here is an example for the knight: 

(deft Knight []
  PieceType
  (image-path [this] (image-asset "knight_white.png"))
  MovablePiece
  (is-valid-move-for-piece?
   [this game-board start-location end-location]
   (and
    (let [direction (map abs (map - end-location start-location))]
      (or (and (= (first direction) 1) (= (second direction) 2))
          (and (= (first direction) 2) (= (second direction) 1))))
    (is-valid-end-location? game-board start-location end-location))))

is-valid-move-for-piece? returns a true-false value of "can my piece move to this square".

This works great for most pieces, but is insufficient for more complicated moves, like castling, where several pieces move at the same time. To handle this, we use another multimethod 

(defmulti special-move-for-piece (fn [x & args] (:type x)))

that is defined only for special moves, and returns the actual state of the modified gameboard.

so for pawns, it would look something like this: 

(defmethod special-move-for-piece ::Pawn
  [this game-board start-location end-location]
  (let [curr-piece-color (::color (get-in (::tiles game-board) start-location))
        move-direction (into [] (map - end-location start-location))
        prev-move (last (::move-history game-board))]
    (cond
      ;; en passant
      (and (= (second move-direction)
              (if (= curr-piece-color ::white)
                1 -1))
           (= (abs (first move-direction)) 1)
         (= (:type (::piece-type (::piece prev-move))) ::Pawn)
         (= (apply max (map abs (map - (::end-location prev-move) (::start-location prev-move)))) 2)
         (= end-location
            (into []
                  (map +
                       (map (fn [x] (/ x 2 )) (map - (::end-location prev-move) (::start-location prev-move)))
                       (::start-location prev-move)))))
      (-> game-board
          (update ::tiles assoc-in start-location nil)
          (update ::tiles assoc-in end-location
                  (get-in (::tiles game-board) start-location))
          (update ::tiles assoc-in (::end-location prev-move)
                  nil))

      (and (is-valid-move-for-piece? this game-board start-location end-location)
           (or (= (second end-location) 0)
               (= (second end-location) 7)))
      (-> game-board
          (update ::tiles assoc-in start-location nil)
          (update ::tiles assoc-in end-location
                  (assoc (get-in (::tiles game-board) start-location)
                         ::piece-type (>Queen))))
      :else nil)))

I'm not going to copy-paste the movesets for every piece in this post, but it was pretty straightforward to define relevant methods for all the different piece types and special-cases, and I'm pretty happy with how the code turned out. When you're reading this code, it really looks like somebody just wrote down all the rules for the game of chess, and that's what makes me feel good, and feel like we've done things in a way that's well organized.

But now, sort of the most important question (for me) is:

is this library actually helping? did deft make our lives better?

I think it did, for the following reasons:

  • deft gives us the features from both protocols/records and multimethods/plain-maps, so we didn't need to decide which tool was right for our use-case. this removes just like a lot of cognitive load, because we can use one tool, and trust that it can do everything pretty well.
  • in particular, it was nice to be able to define :default method dispatch for our protocols, and it was extremely nice to be able to reload protocol method defs from the repl without having to re-instantiate the entire chessboard (and clear the current position)
  • it was really nice to be able to enforce when I wanted method defs to be defined for a particular type, and it was really nice to have an easy way to add Malli schema

Overall, I'm pretty happy with how it all turned out, and I'd say the test of our library was a success.
