Playing around a bit more should get use to realize that there is something awfully wrong here: it doesn’t’ seem possible to solve the above equations using our regular number system – no matter what we try to plug in, our answers always seem to sway far apart from one another. Attempting to come up with feasible solutions using negative numbers doesn’t help either since the multiplication step would require 2 negative numbers and no 2 negative numbers can add up to a number greater than 0.

So – what can we do?

Well – let’s try solving our equation algebraically instead of going through our heuristic approach above. We rearrange our first equation to solve for y:

We substitute this into our 2nd equation to obtain:

We now expand the left hand side:

Let’s move all our terms to the left hand side to get our equation into standard quadratic form:

Finally, we multiply every term by -1 so the squared term is positive:

Taking a glance at the above equation provides us with a bit of a mystery: it doesn’t seem to cross 0 (on our x-axis) at all when we attempt to graph it:

It thus appears that our equation doesn’t have a solution – but let’s try the algebraic approach now to do a quick double check – to do so, we can use the quadratic formula to provide a solution to the above equation. As a reminder, a quadratic equation in the form provided below:

has a solution given by the formula:

From our quadratic formula:

we know that a = 1, b = -6, and c = 36, and we can plug this in to obtain:

This is where we once again encounter a big mystery: the solution to our original quadratic formula appears to take the square root of a negative number (-108) but this is not possible using our regular number system composed of real numbers. We’ve hit a wall.

This exact mathematical wall involving the seemingly impossible square root of a negative number is precisely where the Italian mathematician Gerolamo Cardano found himself in 1545. While developing his groundbreaking general solutions to cubic equations, Cardano noticed something bizarre: even when an equation yielded a completely real, tangible answer, the algebraic path to get there forced him to temporarily calculate the square root of a negative number. For instance, in some of his working expressions, quantities would arise that required manipulating roots like the square root of -15 alongside other terms.

Cardano discovered that if you stubbornly followed the standard rules of algebra with these forbidden quantities—multiplying and simplifying them—the imaginary parts would eventually vanish, leaving behind a perfectly accurate, real-world solution. In fact, in 1545 he published Ars Magna, one of the most important algebra books of the Renaissance. Among its many problems, Cardano asked his readers to divide 10 into two parts whose product was 40. In modern notation, he was searching for two numbers u and v such that:

This should look familiar since it very much resembles our original problem involving x and y. Using a similar approach which we used to turn our original equations into a quadratic one, Cardano simplified the above into the equation shown below:

Applying the quadratic formula leads to a result that would have looked impossible to almost every mathematician of Cardano’s time:

At this point, every instinct from ordinary arithmetic says to stop - you should not be able to take the square root of −15. There is no real number whose square is negative, so the two parts would have to be:

But now something almost magical happens: if we ignore this impossibility for a moment and just apply the usual rules of algebra:

The end product is:

Yet, despite watching the math work out cleanly in front of him, Cardano couldn’t bring himself to believe it. He viewed the whole maneuver as a mere “convenient artifice”— a mathematical magic trick with no actual substance or practical meaning behind it. French philosopher René Descartes (1596–1650) strongly agreed with that skepticism — looking at these strange numbers, Descartes dismissed them as nonsensical fabrications and coined the term imaginary for the roots of negative quantities—a derogatory label meant to mock them as products of pure fancy, which unfortunately stuck around for centuries.

Throughout the 18th century, however, mathematicians found themselves unable to ignore these numbers. They kept popping up as indispensable shortcuts in calculus, algebra, and physics. It was Leonhard Euler who finally gave them a proper home and standard notation, introducing the symbol i to represent the square root of -1:

Even with Euler’s notation, a lingering question remained: what do these numbers actually represent? If real numbers live on a 1-dimensional number line stretching from negative infinity to positive infinity, where do imaginary numbers live?

The answer arrived near the turn of the 19th century when Jean-Robert Argand and Caspar Wessel independently figured out the missing piece of the puzzle: a geometric model. They realized that multiplying by -1 rotates a number 180 degrees on the number line:

Therefore, multiplying by the square root of -1 (or i) shouldn’t just push you further left or right on a one-dimensional line—it represents a 90-degree rotation into a completely new, perpendicular dimension. This is a natural product of i2 being equal to -1 (a 180 degree rotation). Since i represents half of this multiplicative step, it can naturally be mapped to 90 degrees (a halfway 180 degree rotation). By turning our 1D number line into a 2D coordinate plane (where the horizontal axis holds real numbers and the vertical axis holds imaginary numbers), every “complex” number suddenly corresponds to a physical point on a flat plane:

In the above image, the horizontal axis now represents the real number line (-2, -1, 0, 1/3, 3, etc…) while the vertical axis represents a brand new perpendicular dimension representing the real part of our number (-2i, -1i, 0, 1/3i, 3i, etc…). The curved blue line shows what happens when we multiply by i: multiplying +1 by i swings it a quarter turn upward, landing precisely on +i which is a 90 degree rotation.

To put things simply: our new dimension gives us a way to turn our 1-dimensional real number system into a 2-dimensional one. To do this, we allow the regular x-dimension to model the real part of our new number system while the vertical y-dimension now represents the new ‘imaginary’ dimension.

We can visualize this intuitively by taking a look at the diagram below, where a is the real part while b is the imaginary one:

This model provides a natural correspondence between complex numbers and points in the plane. The horizontal axis is called the real axis, the vertical axis the imaginary axis, and an arbitrary complex number z = a + ib appears as the point with coordinates (a, b) on the plane.

We also note that using our new system of dimensions, multiplication by i simply represents a 90 degree rotation:

In the early 1800s, many strict mathematicians rejected the Argand / Wessel plane because it felt like a cheap visual trick. They argued that just because you can draw a picture of the square root of 1 as a vertical line doesn’t prove it logically exists as a number.

In 1833, Hamilton published a paper that removed all geometry and “imaginary” mystery completely. He defined a complex number strictly as an algebraic ordered pair of real numbers, written simply as (a, b). He then defined precise rules for how to add and multiply these pairs:

We can visualize the addition component easily since it maps to regular vector addition:

We can also visualize multiplication (albeit it is a bit less intuitive than addition) by looking at some of the visuals below - in the below visual we multiply an imaginary number by i (to produce a 90 degree rotation):

Another more complex example is provided below where we multiply (2, 1) and (1, 2) in our new imaginary system:

In the above image, we can see an example showing:

Both factors have real and imaginary components. Their directions add together to produce:

and their lengths multiply:

Therefore, the product lands at (0, 5).

This geometric breakthrough was originally popularized and cemented by Carl Friedrich Gauss. Gauss utilized the complex number system to construct the proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra, which demonstrated that every non-constant polynomial equation has at least one root in the complex number system. As an example – even though the graph for the equation below never crosses 0 – we can still find four roots in the complex plane which all appear symmetrically on the unit circle:

That definitive proof finally convinced the wider mathematical community of the profound importance and absolute validity of complex numbers—transforming them from Cardano’s torturous artifice into one of the most powerful tools in all of mathematics and science.

Finally, taking a cue from Cardano and Euler, let’s take that bold leap ourselves and apply this concept to our own unsolved mystery. We left off with the troubling fraction below:

Instead of stopping, we can pull apart that -108. We know that -108 is the exact same as 36 multiplied by -3:

We can evaluate the square root of 36 and pull it outside as a 6:

Here is where Euler’s i comes to the rescue. We can separate out the square root of -1 from the -3:

Substituting in our imaginary unit i and dividing by 2 provides our ultimate, two-part solutions:

Since x + y = 6, the corresponding y-values are:

We write the 2 ordered solutions as:

Let’s check the product:

The two middle terms are equal and opposite, so the imaginary part disappears. The final i² becomes -1, turning the last subtraction into addition. We can visualize this as adding our 2 angles (resulting in a vector of 0 degrees since they are opposite in direction) and scaling our resulting vector (of length 6) by 6 across the x-axis resulting in 36:

We can also easily verify that x + y = 6 since the i components cancel each other out and our real-parts simply add up to equal to 6:

To sum it up – complex numbers are not all that complex: all we’re doing is transforming the number system represented in 1 dimension into a 2-dimensional number. A real number needs only one coordinate, so we draw it on a regular line; a complex number needs two coordinates – a real part and an imaginary part - so we draw it on a plane like the one shown below:

The x-axis above represents our real part while the y-axis represents the imaginary component. Addition now looks like ordinary movement in the plane and we add the real parts horizontally and the imaginary parts vertically.

Multiplication contains an even deeper idea: multiplying by i transforms and the point a + bi into and rotates our 2-dimensional point (or vector) by 90 degrees counter-clockwise:

Multiplying by i a second time turns it another 90 degrees, producing a total rotation of 180 degrees. That is why i squared equals -1: two quarter-turns point us in exactly the opposite direction on the real axis.

Thus, multiplication also maps nicely into this new world (especially when multiplying by i).

Before we explore this connection, it is worth taking a moment to understand what the trigonometric functions actually represent.

At first, sine and cosine are usually introduced as rules involving the sides of a right-angled triangle. Given an angle θ, we define:

Although these definitions are useful, they can make sine and cosine feel like little more than tools for solving triangles. Their deeper meaning becomes much clearer when we place the triangle inside a circle.

Imagine drawing a circle with a radius of 1 and then rotating a line from the positive horizontal axis through an angle θ. The endpoint of that line has two coordinates: a horizontal position and a vertical position. The horizontal coordinate is given by cos θ, while the vertical coordinate is given by sin θ:

Thus the pair:

identifies a point on the unit circle:

As θ changes, the point moves around the circle and the values of sine and cosine keep track of its vertical and horizontal positions.

To put it simply, sine and cosine transform an ANGLE into two directions of movement. Cosine tells us how far we travel horizontally, while sine tells us how far we travel vertically. If our rotating line has a length r instead of 1, these two components become:

This should already look remarkably similar to the complex-number system. A complex number also contains two components: a real component measured horizontally and an imaginary component measured vertically. Trigonometry therefore gives us another way of describing a complex number—not only by stating its horizontal and vertical coordinates, but by stating its LENGTH and ANGLE.

This connection becomes especially powerful when we begin multiplying complex numbers. In the early 18th century, French mathematician Abraham De Moivre noticed a striking similarity between complex multiplication and the addition formulae of the sine and cosine functions from trigonometry. Given that:

it turns out that these two seemingly separate formulae fit together perfectly inside a single complex number. To see why, we first need to look at our complex plane in a slightly different way.

So far, we have described a complex number z = a + bi by giving its horizontal position a and its vertical position b. However, there is another equally useful way to locate the same point. Instead of asking how far right and how far up we travel, we can ask two new questions: how far is the point from the origin, and through what angle must we turn to face it?

We call the distance from the origin r and the angle θ (theta). From the Pythagorean theorem:

and from ordinary trigonometry:

Multiplying both equations by r gives:

We can now substitute these expressions into z = a + bi:

Nothing mysterious has been added here. We have simply changed the language used to describe the point. The form a + bi tells us its horizontal and vertical components, while the form r(cos θ + i sin θ) tells us its length and direction. The first is like giving a street address; the second is like giving a distance and a compass. If r = 1, our point lies on the unit circle and the expression becomes especially simple:

The cosine supplies the horizontal coordinate while the sine supplies the vertical one. As θ changes, the complex number travels around the unit circle. In this form, an angle is no longer merely attached to a complex number—it has become part of the number itself.

Now let’s multiply two unit complex numbers:

Multiplying them in the ordinary algebraic way gives:

Since i² = −1, we can collect the real and imaginary parts:

At first, this result looks a bit cumbersome. But take another look at the two trigonometric addition formulae we started with. The real part is exactly cos(α + β), while the imaginary part is exactly sin(α + β). Therefore:

This is the striking connection which de Moivre uncovered. Complex multiplication automatically performs the angle-addition rules of trigonometry. The large collection of terms created by ordinary algebra is not random at all—it is the sine and cosine addition formula hiding in plain sight.

To put it simply, complex multiplication performs two geometric actions at the same time:

  1. It MULTIPLIES the lengths: r₁ × r₂.

  2. It ADDS the angles: α + β.

Let’s check the picture with an exact algebraic example. Consider:

The trigonometric rule predicts a product with length 2 × 2 = 4 and angle 30° + 60° = 90°:

Ordinary algebra confirms exactly the same thing:

The real terms cancel, leaving a number pointing straight upward on the imaginary axis. The algebra and the geometry are not two different explanations—they are two views of the same multiplication.

Once this pattern is visible, repeated multiplication becomes almost effortless. Multiplying a complex number by itself twice doubles its angle. Multiplying it by itself three times triples its angle. In general, for any whole-number power n:

This is now known as De Moivre’s formula. If the original complex number has a length r, that length is also multiplied by itself n times:

For example, let’s calculate (1 + i)⁴. In rectangular form, 1 + i has:

Therefore:

Applying de Moivre’s formula gives:

Instead of expanding four factors and trying to keep track of every i, we simply raise the length to the fourth power and multiply the angle by four. The number rotates from 45° to 180° while its length grows from √2 to 4.

Another great and simple example which takes the cube of a complex number is provided below:

So De Moivre’s theorem is not just a formula; it is a compact description of rotation. Raising a complex number to the nth power rotates it by n times its original angle.

The same idea can also be run backwards. Powers multiply angles, so roots divide them. However, complex angles contain one final twist: turning through 360° brings us back to the same direction. Thus 0°, 360°, 720°, and every other complete turn all describe the positive real axis.

Suppose we want to solve:

The number 8 has length 8 and angle 0°, but it can also be described using the angles 360° and 720°. Taking the cube root divides the length and each of these angles by three:

This gives three different solutions:

The three answers are equally spaced around a circle. Their angles differ by 120° because 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. More generally, the n different nth roots of a non-zero complex number are evenly spaced around a circle, like the vertices of a perfectly regular polygon. This is one of the reasons complex roots display the beautiful symmetry which we saw earlier in the equation z⁴ + 1 = 0.

We can now see why sine and cosine belong so naturally inside the complex number system. They are not decorative additions placed on top of complex arithmetic. They are the coordinates of rotation itself. Cosine keeps track of the horizontal component, sine keeps track of the vertical component, and complex multiplication combines them in precisely the way required to add angles.

To sum it up – complex numbers were not invented because mathematicians wanted to make arithmetic more complicated – they were invented because ordinary algebra kept producing patterns that the real-number system could not satisfy. What first appeared to be an impossible square root turned out to be evidence that the number line was only a slice of a larger world. Once we allow that world to have two directions instead of one, the mystery begins to disappear: a complex number is not an imaginary answer pretending to exist — it is an ordinary point in a richer mathematical space.

To put it simply, the world of 1-dimensional real numbers turns into a ‘complex’ world involving pairs of reals numbers which are endowed with their own arithmetic. The rectangular form a + bi tells us where a complex number is, while the trigonometric form r(cos θ + i sin θ) tells us how far it reaches and which way it points. Once we use this second language, multiplication becomes scaling plus rotation, powers become repeated rotation, and roots become evenly spaced directions around a circle. What looked like a complicated two-part arithmetic has quietly turned into the geometry of length and angle.

Complex analysis and the use of complex numbers might seem like an abstract idea, but the reality is quite the opposite. Because they are the natural language of rotation, scaling, and oscillation, complex numbers are uniquely equipped to describe the cycles and waves that permeate our physical world. Far from being a mathematical parlor trick, they are an essential tool for engineers, physicists, and computer scientists.

Signal processing and communications are built on the same idea. Any reasonable signal—sound, an image, a radio wave—can be decomposed into a sum of complex exponentials.

The Fourier transform does this, and the fast Fourier transform makes it fast enough for everyday devices. This is how MP3 and JPEG compression work, how WiFi and 5G encode and decode data, how noise-canceling headphones separate unwanted sound, and how radar, GPS, and medical imaging reconstruct information. In each case, complex numbers turn difficult time-domain problems into simpler frequency-domain operations.

Control systems use complex analysis to keep machines stable. Drones, autopilots, robots, cruise control, and thermostats are modeled with Laplace transforms and transfer functions. The poles and zeros of those functions live in the complex plane. Their locations tell engineers whether a system will settle down, oscillate, or become unstable. A pole in the left half-plane usually means stability; a pole on the imaginary axis means sustained oscillation; a pole in the right half-plane means instability. That abstract picture directly determines whether a real machine behaves safely.

Physics and engineering fields rely on complex analysis even more deeply. In electromagnetism, fluid flow, and heat conduction, complex potentials and conformal mappings solve two-dimensional field problems. They are used in aerodynamics to design airfoils, in electrostatics to shape electric fields, and in civil and mechanical engineering to model stresses and flows. Quantum mechanics goes further: the Schrödinger equation contains i explicitly, and wavefunctions are complex-valued. Without complex numbers, modern descriptions of atoms, semiconductors, lasers, and magnetic resonance imaging would be impossible.

So complex numbers are not a strange detour from reality. They are a compact language for rotation and oscillation, and complex analysis is the calculus of that language. The imaginary unit i is not imaginary in the sense of unreal; it is a 90-degree turn. From the AC in our walls to the signals in our phones, from the stability of a drone to the images inside an MRI, the mathematics of complex numbers quietly runs much of the everyday world. What began as an impossible square root became one of the most useful and unifying ideas in science and engineering.

Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model: an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air, entirely on device.

Download for Mac (free) v1.6 · macOS 14+ · Apple Silicon
models download on first launch (715 MB)

Can an embedding model transcribe speech?

EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space. Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word.

So we tried reading words straight out of that space.

How it works

  1. EmbeddingGemma 2's audio encoder stays exactly as it is.
  2. A small reader moves each short slice of audio into the model's text space.
  3. The closest of ~229,000 English words wins, and the slices become a transcript.
  4. A tiny extra model adds punctuation and capitals.

Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech. The base model was never trained for speech-to-text.

item.title: Character.ai Files for Bankruptcy (144 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1009802/character-ai-files-for-bankruptcy-disney, See on Hacker News

Character.AI, one of the first breakout startups of the generative AI boom, has filed for bankruptcy and is selling some of its assets to Disney. The company, which builds various online bots for users to chat or roleplay with, has faced mounting scrutiny and lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, but has continued releasing updates and products in recent months.

In a press release and blog post published Monday, Character said it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets. “Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” the company said.

In its bankruptcy filing, Character listed estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. As part of the proposed sale, Disney would serve as the lead bidder for Character.AI’s assets, setting a baseline for competing offers. Disney would pay $20 million for certain undisclosed assets, and provide transition support “using former Company employees it has hired.” It would also receive a nonexclusive license to unspecified intellectual property.

Disney’s involvement comes shortly after the entertainment behemoth hired Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand as chief technology officer, part of its growing push into AI. Anand’s tenure as Character CEO lasted just over a year and during that time he oversaw the company’s move into microdramas. Disney has previously complained that Character was damaging its brand and exploiting its intellectual property by allowing unauthorized chatbots of its characters, including sending cease and desist letters.

Along with Anand, Disney also said it expected “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” to join the company. The move resembles a kind of “acquihire” strategy that has become increasingly common in Silicon Valley as a means of hoovering up startups’ talent that sometimes leaves the original company struggling to survive. Character.AI has survived it once already — Google spent over $2 billion to hire away much of the company’s talent, including co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, in 2024.

Character said it expects the sale process to be completed by late November or early December and plans to continue operating its services, including paid subscriptions, in the meantime. However, the company warned that “the platform will be wound down” if a suitable bid does not emerge. “As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority,” it said.

item.title: Crypto thieves sell hardware wallets with secret eSIM (110 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.heise.de/en/news/Crypto-thieves-sell-hardware-wallets-with-secret-eSIM-11485188.html, See on Hacker News

  1. Crypto thieves sell hardware wallets with secret eSIM
    • LTE modem calls home
    • Secret change of ownership at dealer
    • Series production

“The Ledger Nano X is the most secure way to manage your cryptocurrency,” advertises the French company Ledger, its hardware wallet for cryptocurrencies. Nevertheless, users have lost around 100 million US dollars in cryptocurrencies. This is because unknown individuals have succeeded in intercepting and manipulating the offline wallets while on the go.

Each Ledger Nano X has a Secure Element chip that controls a tiny touchscreen. Ledger praises this as particularly secure. Unfortunately, this only applies if attackers cannot read the screen. This is exactly what the perpetrators are doing. They insert additional hardware into apparently genuine Ledger Nano X and then sell them to unsuspecting crypto speculators.

If buyers use such a modified hardware wallet and create a seed phrase with it, the attackers automatically read along. They haven’t touched the Secure Element chip at all; it remains secure. Instead, they have installed an additional chip that intercepts the transmission from the Secure Element to the built-in screen and recognizes the displayed letters of the seed phrase – embedded Tempest. This is indicated by an analysis by Tibane Labs.

LTE modem calls home

Recognizing the characters alone doesn’t help the perpetrators yet, because the wallets fundamentally work offline. So the perpetrators have also installed an LTE modem, a tiny eSIM module, and a small antenna, all powered by the accumulator already built into the hardware wallet. Thus, the seed phrase is transmitted via mobile phone to the perpetrators, who thus gain control over the cryptocurrency assets secured by the seed phrase.

Ledger has admitted to one customer that they suffered financial loss and that their hardware wallet was manipulated. However, the company has not yet confirmed the exact circumstances and the full extent of the damage. Blockchain observers state that they have identified over 300 affected wallets so far, which have been collectively depleted of approximately 93 million US dollars. The stolen cryptocurrency units are subsequently exchanged and, at least in part, laundered through crypto mixers.

Secret change of ownership at dealer

Suspicion is directed at Cryptobilis, a wallet dealer operating primarily in Southeast Asia from Malaysia. Anyone who has purchased from Cryptobilis in the last three months should not use these wallets and should quickly move any existing holdings to another wallet, Ledger advises. It prohibits Cryptobilis from making further sales for now. All Ledger dealers are prohibited from offering any returns to other customers.

Unfortunately, not every affected buyer knows that they bought from Cryptobilis. Tibane Labs reports a manipulated Ledger device that was purchased via Amazon Japan from a Chinese seller but was mailed in Malaysia.

In the crypto scene, it is said that Cryptobilis recently received new owners without this being announced. The previous owners reportedly state they have nothing more to do with their old company. According to unverified screenshots, the wallet dealer has belonged to a Chinese man named JiaMing since August. Depending on the pronunciation, this is a common name in China or means “wrong name”.

Series production

The recently discovered manipulated Ledger devices are at least the third generation. In May, embedded specialist Joe Grand presented at the Hardware.io conference, apparently Ledger Nano[ ]X still manipulated by hand. To make space in the small USB stick, the perpetrators replaced the accumulator with a much smaller one and created conspicuous wiring – conspicuous, of course, only if you take the USB stick apart, which users don’t usually do.

Tibane Labs now describes wallets of two further advanced manipulation generations. One was already more professionally designed but still replaced the battery. In the third known generation, added parts are precisely cut in professional series production, and the original battery is untouched.

The perpetrators have found another, less conspicuous way: Ledger protects the built-in screen from below with foam. The attackers scratch this away and thus create space for their additional hardware. Anyone who opens the casing will see nothing other than unmanipulated Ledger Nano X, except for a small antenna wire.

item.title: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey (317 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.thehistoryblog.com/archives/77107, See on Hacker News

Archaeologists have uncovered a royal archive of cuneiform tablets in the ancient Hittite city of Samuha, modern-day Sivas, central Turkey. This year’s excavation unearthed 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments which record an epidemic of fever, military logistics, religious practices and events of royal daily life 3,400 years ago. Last year’s excavation uncovered 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments, so this season’s discoveries more than triple the number of texts. It is now the largest, most comprehensive archive of Hittite-language documents found in the 21st century.

The records date to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, and are written in Hittite and Hurrian. One text tells of a fever epidemic that struck the infant daughter of the king. She was still a nursing baby when she became ill. She never recovered from the fever and her health declined precipitously until she passed away. The cuneiform tablet records the funerary ritual that followed.

The health of the princes and princesses, not just babies but even up to adulthood, was an important focus of the records. The children of high-ranking imperial officials were given the same attention. Because illness was considered an expression of divine will, religious leaders performed many rituals to keep an eye on the physical health of the children of kings and government officials.

Another notable document is a letter from Hittite generals in western Anatolia appealing to the king for reinforcements in men, horses and chariots to fend off enemy forces. The generals’ warnings are dire. They plead that without an infusion of strength, the army would be destroyed by the enemy. They have the temerity to disclaim all responsibility for any upcoming failures if the reinforcements don’t come.

It’s a rare glimpse into the realities of military logistics with armies long distances from the king and court. The text also confirms that the king was at Samuha when the letter arrived, underscoring the city’s political importance. It was a royal stronghold for King Tudhaliya during times of military and political upheaval. His successor Suppiluliuma I used it as a launching pad for military campaigns that consolidated and expanded the territory of the Hittite Empire.

Samuha was also a major center of religious administration. Its patron deity was the goddess Sauska, goddess of love and war who was the Hurrian version of Ishtar and the most important goddess in the Hurrian pantheon. The association with the goddess was central to the city’s identity and was reflected in its religious ceremonies.

One tablet records the journeys of bird diviners who left Samuha and traveled through different regions. Their routes, the cities where they stayed and the birds they observed were recorded in a format resembling a diary. The documents also provide previously unknown information about how bird omens were observed, evaluated and interpreted by the Hittites.

The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture.

item.title: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF (104 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks, See on Hacker News

The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.

In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit.

Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.”

An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.

It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”.

The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.

“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said.

Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”.

The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.

Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”.

The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.

Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies.

The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.

In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.

In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said.

It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.

It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.

In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats.

He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems.

“One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

item.title: A look at OpenAI’s math that’s claimed computes faster Fourier transforms (231 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.argmin.net/p/faster-fourier-transforms, See on Hacker News

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post looks at part of OpenAI’s math repository that claims to compute faster Fourier transforms. It’s more technical than usual, but I tried to add some tutorial material for people who need a refresher course on signal processing or computational complexity.

The Fast Fourier Transform is one of the most important innovations in digital signal processing and one of my favorite algorithms. The FFT is a fast way to extract the frequency content of signals, letting you rapidly analyze, filter, and manipulate frequencies across different bands of the spectrum.

The Fourier transform computes the energy in each frequency band through a simple dot product.1 Let x denote your input, a length n array of samples, and f a frequency. Then the amount of frequency content in x at f can be computed by the formula:

For digital signals, a bit of math shows you only need to compute n of these dot products, one at each multiple of the frequency 2𝜋/n, to understand all of the frequency content. Naively, this requires n multiplications and additions for each frequency. Hence, computing the entire Fourier transform appears to require n2 arithmetic operations.

The fast Fourier transform is a clever recursive procedure devised by James Cooley and John Tukey in 1965.2 The main idea is that a length-n Fourier transform can be computed by shuffling the input vector, computing two Fourier transforms of length n/2 on the shuffled components, and then recombining the outputs using atomic arithmetic operations. The shuffles and recombinations take a linear number of arithmetic operations. Repeating this procedure iteratively, namely, log2(n) times, computes the full discrete Fourier transform. With the bookkeeping, the FFT computes a length-n Fourier transform in fewer than 5 n log2 n arithmetic operations.

To make this acceleration concrete, when n is 1,000, n^2 is 1,000,000 and 5 * n log n is around 50,000, a 20-fold speedup. When n is 1,000,000, the speedup is 10,000-fold. These speedups can be the difference between a transform being computable or not given the constraints of a signal processing application.

Since the invention of the FFT, people have looked for even faster Fourier transforms. One question is just how fast you can go. It seems like you probably need at least n operations to compute the FFT, as it takes n steps just to write it down. The FFT is 5*log2(n) times slower than that reasonable speed limit, and that 5*log2(n) factor can be big. It’s 200 when n is a trillion. Can you do something clever to reduce that prefactor of 200?

Well, lo and behold, in the massive paper dump OpenAI took on the mathematics world last week, they claim to have a faster Fourier transform. The main claim from their discriminatively named “main.pdf” is

I was intrigued about what was going on here. The log(n) term, in theory, was a teeny tiny bit smaller than in the standard FFT.

Did I read this paper? Of course not. No one at OpenAI read this paper either, so why should I? I did what every other mathematician in the world does with AI slop mathematics: I fed it back into the slop machine and ran an information retrieval session with a chatbot interface to extract salient facts. Anthropomorphically speaking: I asked ChatGPT what it thinks about its own output. This is how we do mathematical research now. What a world.

Unfortunately, I did not find a faster Fourier transform. Instead,l I found the rot that develops inside applied mathematical theory when formalism becomes so detached from reality that a “breakthrough” is nothing more than an artifact of mathematicians not being able to properly specify the rules of their games in natural language.

First, “big-O” notation has been so abused that it has become meaningless. Let’s review the definition, which impressed me as an undergrad. An algorithm has running time T(n) = O(F(n)) if there exists an integer N and a constant C such that

That is, the number of steps the algorithm actually takes is upper bounded by a constant times some convenient function F(n) as long as n is large. F(n) is usually something familiar and interpretable, like a polynomial or exponential function. This notation says that we only care about what happens when the size of the computation is large. We care about the asymptotic growth rate of the computation time. All constants are equivalent.

Big-O notation is useful for shortcuts in algorithmic accounting, but it also allows for remarkable logical laziness. If we want a practically faster FFT, we want an algorithm that requires fewer than 50n operations for reasonably sized n. But O(n) does not mean 50 n. It could mean 1080 n. This would be considered a “linear time” algorithm. An algorithm that requires n + 1080 is also considered a linear time algorithm in the big-O regime. An algorithm that only has linear-time guarantees when n is greater than 1080 is also considered linear time. 1080 is approximately equal to the number of atoms in the known universe. That is why Richard Lipton and Ken Regan call algorithms with unfathomably large hidden constants galactic algorithms.

The OpenAI FFT algorithm is definitely galactic. The estimated values for C were 10100 when N=1012. So even when n=10100, the venerable Cooley-Tukey-Gauss FFT would be 1099 times faster.

So why is this new FFT result interesting? Well, note that in big-O notation, it is technically asymptotically faster than the Cooley-Tukey algorithm because

I mean, sure. But given the constants, the algorithm runs faster only when n is impossibly large. Roughly, you need

whatever the hell that number means.

Lipton and Regan argue galactic algorithms are useful because they spur research. Once you show a running time is asymptotically possible, you can spend your time finding an algorithm that practically achieves this provable running time. Maybe you can send your AI agent swarms after it. You do you. Maybe you can get a practical algorithm out, but I don’t know of any legitimate examples where this happened. I’m particularly doubtful here, because the model of “computation” OpenAI uses bears no resemblance to an actual computer.

“The model uses exact complex arithmetic.” That means it assumes you can store and multiply complex numbers at arbitrary precision. Indeed, the algorithm requires you to multiply complex numbers whose magnitudes grow superpolynomially with n. If you stored these numbers as bits, the memory requirement would effectively be exponential in the input length. It assumes you can multiply such arbitrarily large complex numbers together in a single operation. We do not have computers that can do this. So even if this theorem in main.pdf is “true” (no one knows, and I don’t care), it’s not actually solving the problem we set out to solve when looking for a faster FFT.

For people familiar with theoretical analyses of the FFT, that you need an absurd model of computation to break the FFT speed limit isn’t surprising. In 1973, Jacques Morgenstern proved that you couldn’t get a Fourier transform faster than ½ n log n if you required that complex coefficients used in the computation had bounded magnitude. That should have been the end of the story! But it wasn’t. People said Morgenstern’s restricted coefficient model was too restrictive. Forty years later, Nir Ailon showed that you couldn’t compute an FFT faster than n log n without severe numerical instabilities. This was also too restrictive for some people, I guess.

This new OpenAI result is thus less a mathematical breakthrough and more an oddity of computer scientists being bad at formalizing their design specifications. The “theoretical” definition of a computer is very far removed from the computers we actually build. The “faster” Fourier transform is merely an example where theory gets so unmoored from the original question that an “open problem” becomes nothing more than an academic status puzzle. The solution is like what happens when you set computational bot streams at impossible problems and find them engaging in illegal hacking.

Many of the other “big” results in this OpenAI slopository could be critiqued in the same way. For example, one of those results was a galactic algorithm to multiply two matrices in O(n^2.25) operations. The construction used in the paper does not let you even estimate the constant that hides inside big O.3 It may as well be infinite, computable only with the divine music of the spheres.

Still, if written substantially better, these papers would have made it into the most prestigious publication venues for the theory of computer science (i.e., refereed conference proceedings from STOC or FOCS).4 The matrix multiplication paper would have likely won awards. But neither of these has anything to do with computers!

This is because the theory of computer science has a culture that actively discourages running algorithms on a computer. It’s acceptable to write papers in theory conferences that assert an algorithm exists without ever writing it down. The theory of computer science has become a form of mathematics that doesn’t concern itself with computers, and it offers little reward for impact outside those mathematical pursuits. I explained this to a friend who remarked to me that “theory” has the transdisciplinary meaning of “hiding in obscurity of one’s own making.”

AI is really good at automating our worst tendencies. It amplifies the unspoken cultural practices no one likes, but no individual can reasonably deviate from. It exploits the mechanized traditions recalcitrant to collective action. In that vein, AI can now write useless theory papers. But perhaps in the absurdity of the distasteful OpenAI trash dump of proofs, we can all look up and realize together that we should consider doing something else.

The industry at the moment wants people who know how to use AI to further the business goals but here’s the thing nobody wants to admit: not one person knows how to use AI to actually do that. I use it to write a lot of my code and then I critically review that code before it reaches production.

My life is based here in Warrnambool and I choose to work remotely from here. Hybrid is infeasible even if it were in Melbourne because Melbourne is 3.5hrs away on the train. I know I can work remotely effectively because I did it for the last 6 years. And I helped others adjust to that as well!

item.description:
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13928, See on Hacker News

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

item.title: Show HN: SolidCraft – Open-Source Parametric CAD in Rust (With MCP Support) (119 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft, See on Hacker News

An open-source parametric 3D CAD application built in pure Rust.

Sketch, constrain, and build solids with a parametric feature timeline. Change a dimension and watch your model rebuild. Run it on your desktop, in your browser, or let AI agents model through the built-in MCP server.

A Raspberry Pi 4 case from an empty design: a sketch dimensioned with the board's parameters, extrude, fillet, shell, the rim rounded in one pick, an M2.5 standoff patterned on the 58 × 49 mm hole rectangle, port cut-outs, vent slots, "Pi 4" engraved in DejaVu Sans Bold and a PETG material defined in the design, with its mass in Properties, then height 24 → 32 mm in Parameters and it all rebuilds. 9× playback. Full video, recorded with the demo script.

Download

  • Windows: download and run the installer. Also for ARM64 and 32-bit PCs, or as a portable zip that runs without installing.
  • macOS: open the disk image and drag SolidCraft into Applications (Apple silicon and Intel).
  • Linux: download the AppImage, allow it to run as a program and open it. Or install the .deb (Ubuntu, Debian, Mint) or .rpm (Fedora, openSUSE), or use Flatpak. With Snap: sudo snap install solidcraft (Snap Store, or the .snap file). For ARM64: AppImage, .deb, .rpm.
  • Web: try it in your browser, no install.

The downloads aren't signed yet. On Windows, if SmartScreen warns you, choose More info, then Run anyway. On macOS, the first time, right-click SolidCraft in Applications and choose Open.

Older versions, checksums and other formats are on the releases page. Install details, upgrading from earlier builds and building from source are in Getting started.

Documentation: the SolidCraft book (user guide, developer guide and command reference; sources in docs/book).

Status: early but usable for simple parts. 75 of 76 public reference parts match their analytic or FreeCAD-computed volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box (docs/oracle.md); the other is a tracked bug. These checks do not establish complete geometric or workflow equivalence. The commands SolidCraft has are listed by area in docs/features.md; status and plans are in ROADMAP.md. Open work and known bugs are in GitHub issues, and help is welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md.

Built with SolidCraft

SELENE, a scientific rover built entirely through SolidCraft's MCP server by @0xlillith: 3,323 editable timeline steps that rebuild with no errors, replayed here at 2× speed. Full video · download the editable model.

What works

  • Sketches on origin planes, offset planes or planar faces: lines, rectangles, circles, arcs, polygons, slots, ellipses, fit/control splines, conics and text; construction geometry, projection, trimming, fillets and chamfers, including corners at the origin. New face attachments retain supported construction identities and chosen occurrences; missing sources expose an explicit plane repair workflow. See face attachments. Explicitly closed fit splines and closed associative offsets use periodic C2 interpolation. Supported convex line-and-arc offsets retain their identity when an inset consumes corner arcs, and linked extrusions follow the current boundary. Breaking the association freezes the boundary and keeps existing extrusions usable. Curve drawing and picking adapt together to zoom and display scale, including small circles at Fit and sketches in placed components.
  • Constraints and dimensions solved by our own solver. Points the constraints fix relative to known geometry are placed exactly by construction (loci intersections and rigid-cluster decomposition, after Owen 1991 and Fudos–Hoffmann 1997); Levenberg–Marquardt solves the rest, and the rank of its Jacobian gives the remaining degrees of freedom. Constraints: coincident, point on curve, horizontal/vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, curvature (G2), equal, concentric, collinear, midpoint, symmetry, fix; linear, aligned, horizontal, vertical, point-to-line, radius, diameter, angle, arc sweep, arc length and slot length dimensions driven by parameters. Over-constraining edits are rejected; fully constrained geometry turns black. Dragging solves the sketch every frame and rebuilds the model once, when the drag ends. Select a line or its two endpoints, type its dimension and press Enter to commit one undo step; with Sketch Dimension it's D, click, type, Enter. Fit keeps sketch geometry clear of the palette and navigation controls.
  • Profiles found automatically, including regions split by lines and holes inside outlines. Newly captured complete adaptive boundaries retain their outer and hole source identities when spline span counts change. Partial or ambiguous boundaries do not qualify.
  • Features on a parametric timeline: extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet/chamfer, shell, draft, holes, threads, patterns, mirror, split, combine, move and construction geometry. The timeline rebuilds incrementally; features can be edited, suppressed, renamed, reordered and deleted. Supported geometry and current limitations are described in ROADMAP.md. New revolves preserve symmetric and two-sided angular placement across reversed axes; older designs retain their saved convention when reopened or edited.
  • Parameters and configurations with unit-aware expressions (2 * width + 5 mm, angle / 2), ordered rules, feature suppression and per-row body materials/appearances.
  • Assemblies with nested components and occurrences, joints, motion studies, contact sets, interference and material-aware mass properties. Recorded body transfers preserve modelling history and world placement; 3D sketch wires retain their coordinate frames through edits.
  • Sheet metal with flanges, hems, fold/unfold/refold, material cutouts, flat patterns, retained shallow prismatic pockets, exact line/arc/circle DXF outlines and bend tables; plastic enclosure features and rules. Pocket depth and side survive unfold/refold and appear separately from through-hole outlines in the flat preview and DXF.
  • Files: design containers (.solidcraft) with lossless binary mesh payloads; plain JSON remains supported for opening, Save As and export. Desktop Open can show a saved provisional picture from warm geometry caches while rebuilding before editing; caches never replace the parametric design. Export to STEP (AP242 with body names, colours and components as assemblies; revolved faces as native planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori), IGES 5.3 (manifold solid B-reps with names and colours), 3MF, STL (binary/ASCII) and OBJ; 3MF, STL and OBJ import as mesh bodies (they render, measure, move and export; solid features need B-rep bodies). Convert Mesh reconstructs supported closed constant-section parts as parametric solids with planar and circular cylindrical faces; STEP import (AP203/AP214/AP242 solids, assemblies, units, names, colours) and IGES import (manifold solid B-reps, or trimmed and bounded surfaces sewn into solids) as a base feature that later features build on — open a .step/.stp/.igs/.iges file, insert one into a design, or drop it on the window (docs/step-import.md).
  • Desktop app (egui + wgpu): toolbar with workspace tabs, browser, timeline, 3D viewport with axis view and navigation bar, sketch tools, feature dialogs, command palette, and a JSON-lines control channel so agents and tests can drive it. Feature errors and Help can open an editable Create Issue draft with relevant context and an optional reviewed screenshot; opening GitHub does not submit the report.
  • Headless CLI solidcraft-cli: run command scripts, measure (volume, area, centre of mass, face/edge/vertex counts), export, render PNG snapshots and replay reference recipes.
  • MCP server solidcraft-cli mcp: AI agents model, measure and look at parts headless or in the running app (see below).

Build and run

cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample          # desktop app with a sample part
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- commands      # the command registry
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- run examples/bracket.json --out bracket.step
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- snapshot examples/bracket.json --out bracket.png
cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- part.step          # open a STEP file as a new design
cargo run --release -p solidcraft-cli -- eval part.step # measure an imported STEP file
cargo xtask ci                                          # fmt, clippy, tests, assets, layers, wasm

Windows builds: cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p solidcraft.

On Windows and Linux, SolidCraft detects a connected 3Dconnexion SpaceNavigator or SpaceMouse through its multi-axis HID interface. Move the cap to pan and zoom, and tilt or twist it to rotate the 3D view. While editing a sketch, the cap pans and zooms without changing the sketch view. The Navigation page in Preferences has an on/off switch and a speed control for the 3D mouse.

On Linux SolidCraft reads /dev/hidrawN directly, so the logged-in user needs access to the device. A udev rule that adds the uaccess tag does that, for example /etc/udev/rules.d/70-3d-mouse.rules for devices with 3Dconnexion's vendor id:

SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", ATTRS{idVendor}=="256f", TAG+="uaccess"

Older SpaceNavigators use Logitech's vendor id 046d; add a rule with their product id (see lsusb) instead of matching every Logitech device. Reload with sudo udevadm control --reload && sudo udevadm trigger, then replug the device. The Flatpak sandbox does not expose hidraw devices, so the 3D mouse only works with native builds there for now. Devices that send all six axes in HID report 1 (some homemade ones do) are recognised from their report descriptor, so they work as well.

In the browser: cd apps/solidcraft-web && trunk build --release --public-url ./ (WebGPU, or WebGL2 with ?webgl; ?sample opens the sample part).

Scripts

A script is a JSON list of commands, the same ones the UI runs:

{"commands": [
  {"command": "sketch.create", "params": {"plane": "XY"}},
  {"command": "sketch.rectangle.two_point", "params": {"p0": [0, 0], "p1": [40, 30]}},
  {"command": "solid.extrude", "params": {"distance": 20}},
  {"command": "solid.fillet", "params": {"edges": [[0, 0, 10]], "radius": 3}}
]}

AI agents (MCP)

solidcraft-cli mcp is a Model Context Protocol server on stdio. Headless it runs its own design session; with --connect 127.0.0.1:PORT it drives the app started with solidcraft --control PORT, so you can watch the agent model. item.title: I turned my unused Kindle into a photo frame with GPT-6 Astra (144 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nirajrajgor.com/blog/kindle-photo-frame-with-ai, See on Hacker News

My Kindle was sitting unused, so I decided to see whether AI could help me find a new use for it. I wanted to create a custom app that could cover a range of uses and be controlled by an AI agent on my MacBook.

I started with a small goal: use my own image as the Kindle's screensaver. Once that worked, I asked the agent to build an app that could cycle through a collection of photos.

We called the project KindleCTL. On my Kindle, I open "Photo Slideshow" from the same screen where I choose my books. It cycles through ten photos, showing each for four minutes. When I want to read, I exit the slideshow and return to my books.

I used Codex and T3 Code on my Mac to work with the coding agents.

I first tried GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning effort set to Extra High. It wrote code to connect to the Kindle but couldn't resolve an error that prevented it from storing data on the device. Then I tried Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, but Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards blocked each attempt after two prompts. Finally, I tried GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to High. We were able to jailbreak the Kindle.

We used the existing jailbreak code as a reference to build our own tools for running custom software on the Kindle. Then we created and installed the slideshow app.

The slideshow passed its automated checks on my Mac, but switching photos on the Kindle left traces of the previous image on screen. The tests hadn't caught how the physical display refreshed. Getting from passing tests to something I could use turned out to be the most interesting part of the experiment.

Let's walk through how we went from an unused Kindle to a working photo frame, starting with getting the agent connected.

Connecting the agent to the Kindle

I started in an empty project folder with a 10th-generation Kindle Basic. I gave the agent its network address and device details. We had no USB connection, so the entire setup happened over Wi-Fi.

From there, we still needed to set up access to run our own software on the Kindle.

The GPT-5.6 Sol attempt got as far as loading a helper on the Kindle, but the program that helper was meant to start never reported that it was ready to execute. It couldn't locate a filesystem where it could store content.

The attempts with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were both blocked by Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards after two prompts. Then I tried GPT-6 Astra. I explicitly asked it to build the custom software we needed for personal use and take inspiration from existing open-source projects.

We adapted the existing jailbreak from SpiderCat, released by sparklerfish and the KindleModding community, and built custom tools called KindleCTL around it.

  • What we built: Tools to send commands from my Mac, transfer files, and investigate errors on the Kindle.
  • What broke: Our launcher crashed before it could start. We traced that to a compatibility issue with the Kindle's older system software and fixed how the launcher was built.
  • How we checked: We connected with administrator access, transferred files both ways, and displayed text. Later, we verified that access still worked after a reboot.

The feedback loop was the game changer

Initially, the agent could connect to the Kindle but couldn't display data. To debug this, it asked me for pictures of the Kindle's screen. I took photos with my phone and shared them with the agent on my Mac.

This was becoming tedious. Since the agent was connected to the Kindle, I wondered why it couldn't get this information itself. I asked it to set up a feedback loop so it could access logs without me having to share screenshots.

The agent set up a persistent diagnostic connection so it could collect errors and test fixes without asking me to download and reopen a package each time. Later, we added remote screen captures so it could also inspect what the Kindle was displaying.

This was a turning point that let the agent continue implementing changes on autopilot. Its reasoning traces showed it figuring out which folders survived a restart and which could store external data.

I was surprised the agent hadn't suggested this on its own. Once I asked for a feedback loop, it set one up and could test fixes without my help.

Most of the code was written in Python. The Kindle's launcher and slideshow were written in C, with shell scripts handling installation and device controls.

With the connection working, I asked the agent to try a small test first: transfer an image and set it as the Kindle's screensaver. I checked that the image appeared correctly and that waking the Kindle brought back the normal Home screen. Once that worked, I asked for the slideshow app.

Getting the slideshow working

I asked the agent for a looping slideshow of ten photos, with an Exit button. Each photo would fit the screen while keeping its original aspect ratio.

The slides were changing, but the transitions weren't smooth, so I asked the agent to look into it. With the feedback loop already in place, it investigated the issue and used the Kindle's built-in screen refresh mechanism to clear the previous image after each slide change.

The screen captures showed complete images, but they couldn't reveal traces left on the physical display. After the refresh change, I checked the Kindle and confirmed that each photo looked clean.

I customized how long each photo stays on screen and the brightness level. If the Kindle goes to sleep, the slideshow picks up where it left off when it wakes.

For now, I use my Mac to change the photos and slideshow timing. The photos stay stored on the Kindle, so the slideshow works without Wi-Fi. In the future, we could add controls to change the slideshow timing on the Kindle and send photos directly from a phone or another device.

What I learned

Next time, I'd set up the feedback loop from the start so the agent could read logs, inspect screen captures, and test fixes on the device.

The Kindle now sits on our wooden shelf, where we use it every day as a photo frame.

I started because I was curious about what AI could help me do with an unused device. Now I have an app for my photos that works the way I asked, plus the tools to keep experimenting with the Kindle.

Disclaimer: This was a personal experiment on my own Kindle, not a step-by-step jailbreak guide. Only experiment with devices you own or have explicit permission to modify.
